title: Koko Eating Bananas
prompt:
Koko has `piles` of bananas and `h` hours before the guards return. Each hour she picks one pile and eats `k` bananas from it; if the pile has fewer than `k`, she eats them all and waits out the rest of that hour. Return the **minimum** integer speed `k` that lets her finish every pile within `h` hours.

**Example 1**: `piles = [3,6,7,11]`, `h = 8` → `4`

**Example 2**: `piles = [30,11,23,4,20]`, `h = 5` → `30`

**Example 3**: `piles = [30,11,23,4,20]`, `h = 6` → `23`

**Constraints**: `1 <= piles.length <= 10^4`, `piles.length <= h <= 10^9`, `1 <= piles[i] <= 10^9`.

tests.note: h == piles: must clear each pile in one hour
big piles — watch int overflow in the hour count

hints: If Koko can finish at speed k, can she also finish at speed k + 1? What does that tell you about the set of speeds that work?
Speeds 1..max(piles) line up as fail…fail, work…work. Search that range for the first speed where a quick simulation says total hours ≤ h, halving the range each time.
Hours for one pile at speed k is a ceiling: `(pile + k - 1) / k`. Sum them in a `long` — 10⁴ piles of 10⁹ at speed 1 overflows int.

solution.explanation: Binary search on the answer. Feasibility is monotonic — any speed faster than a working speed also works — so the lower-bound template (`hi = mid` when feasible, `lo = mid + 1` otherwise) converges on the smallest feasible speed. Speed max(piles) always works because h ≥ piles.length. O(n log max(piles)) time, O(1) space.
